00 / Lab overview

Tenstorrent programming lab

01 / Architecture

Tenstorrent architecture

A Tenstorrent accelerator contains many Tensix cores, each with local memory and compute engines. This chapter follows data from the host through device DRAM, the on-chip network, and one core.

In this chapter
Architecture generationsBoard specificationsQuerying and managing devicesThe multicore deviceInside one Tensix coreMemory hierarchyNetwork on chip (NoC)Tile layout in DRAM and L1Destination registers (DST)

Architecture generations

The four architecture families covered here are Grayskull, Wormhole, Blackhole, and Quasar.

FamilyHardware documentation
GrayskullFirst-generation Tensix family; retained in the legacy hardware documentation.
WormholePCIe cards include n150 and n300. The public ISA manual describes the B0 stepping.
BlackholePCIe cards include p100a, p150a, and p150b. The public ISA manual describes the A0 stepping.
QuasarThe official simulator repository describes Quasar as pre-silicon and provides simulator binaries.

The multicore device

The host CPU prepares inputs and launches work through PCIe. GDDR6 memory holds device tensors. A network on chip (NoC) carries data between memory controllers, Tensix cores, and other endpoints. Each Tensix core has its own L1 SRAM and arithmetic engines.

A matrix can be divided into output blocks and distributed across the cores. Each core fetches the input blocks it needs into its local memory, computes its assigned outputs, and transfers the results back to DRAM. Cores can also transfer data directly to one another.

Read the source: Metalium architecture introduction ↗ · Blackhole NoC ↗

Inside one Tensix core

“Baby RISC-V” means a small control CPU. Tenstorrent uses the nickname for five compact, 32-bit processors inside each Tensix core: B, NC, T0, T1, and T2. Each executes a program with instructions, registers, loops, and branches. Their design emphasizes low area and power.

Packers, unpackers, and math engines are separate execution units. The RISC-V processors issue commands to them. For example, T2 runs the control code that tells a packer which destination tile to format and write into L1; the packer performs the transfer. T1 issues arithmetic commands to the matrix engine or vector engine (SFPU), which perform the numerical work.

The matrix engine (FPU) multiplies and accumulates tiles. The vector engine (SFPU) performs elementwise and special-function operations. Both use destination registers (DST) to hold compute results. Unpackers bring operands from L1 into compute registers; packers format results and write them to L1.

Resource per core (Wormhole B0 / Blackhole A0)Count and function
Small RISC-V control CPUs (“Baby”)5 programmable processors: B, NC, T0, T1, and T2. Execute control code and issue commands to the engines.
Unpackers2 engines for operand loading and format conversion.
Matrix engine / FPU1 engine for matrix arithmetic.
Vector engine / SFPU1 engine; 32 SIMD lanes, each 32 bits wide.
Scalar unit / ThCon1 unit; integer scalar operations and 128-bit L1 memory operations.
Packers4 engines for writing compute results to L1.
NoC interfaces2 connections per core.

B and NC run the data-movement kernels: they issue NoC transfers between L1, DRAM, and other cores. T0 issues unpack instructions; T1 issues matrix and vector math instructions; T2 issues pack instructions. The dashed arrows show this usual software assignment. The hardware provides shared execution resources, so the assignment is established by the kernel software.

Memory hierarchy

L1 is software-managed scratchpad SRAM. Each core keeps its current operands, intermediate buffers, and code there. The unpack and pack engines move tensor values between L1 and the compute registers.

StorageWormhole B0Blackhole A0
L1 SRAM per Tensix core1,464 KiB = 1,499,136 bytes1,536 KiB = 1,572,864 bytes
BF16 tile payload2 KiB for 32×32 values2 KiB for 32×32 values
Available L1 buffer budgetProgram- and runtime-dependentProgram- and runtime-dependent
Destination registers (DST) per core32 KiB total32 KiB total
Full DST, 16-bit elements16,384 values = 16 standard tiles16,384 values = 16 standard tiles
Full DST, 32-bit elements8,192 values = 8 standard tiles8,192 values = 8 standard tiles

Available buffer space is the L1 region left for a program after firmware, code, and runtime reservations. The compiler places input queues, output queues, intermediate buffers, and communication state within that budget. Existing allocations and alignment reduce the space left for another buffer.

TT-Lang checks the combined per-core allocation with ttl-validate-cb-budget and subsequent lowering checks. The target supplies the default budget; --ttl-l1-budget N overrides it in bytes. Use the budget configured for the course runner when sizing buffers. Increasing this option only changes the compiler limit; physical memory and runtime reservations stay the same.

remaining budget = configured L1 buffer budget − planned allocations BF16 tile payloads that fit ≤ floor(remaining budget / 2,048)

The tile calculation is an upper bound before any additional alignment or placement constraints. DST has its own separate 32 KiB register capacity.

Read the source: TT-Lang L1 budget checks ↗ · L1 capacities ↗ · Destination register organization ↗ · Blackhole destination registers ↗

Network on chip (NoC)

A NoC is the communication network inside the accelerator. Routers forward packets between endpoints. An endpoint may expose a core’s L1 memory, a DRAM controller, or another device resource. A transfer identifies both the destination endpoint and an address within it.

Wormhole and Blackhole have two physically separate NoCs. Each forms a two-dimensional torus: rows and columns connect back to their opposite edges. The two networks connect the same endpoints and send packets in opposite directions.

A DRAM read returns data to the requesting core’s L1. A core-to-core write sends bytes from one L1 to another. Multicast sends a payload to several destination cores. The destination must have free storage, and consumers wait for transfer completion before reading the received data.

Packets travel in fixed-size units called flits. Blackhole doubles the flit width compared with Wormhole.

Network propertyWormhole B0Blackhole A0
Physical NoCs22
Packet flit size256 bits = 32 bytes512 bits = 64 bytes
Transfer operationsReads, writes, atomicsReads, writes, atomics

Read the source: Wormhole NoC ↗ · Blackhole NoC and official topology figures ↗

Tile layout in DRAM and L1

This layout describes the bytes of a tiled tensor buffer in device DRAM or L1 SRAM. Copying an intact tile between these memories preserves its byte order. The unpacker converts stored values into the representation used by compute registers.

A standard tile covers 32×32 scalar values. Its four 16×16 faces are stored in sequence: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right. Within each face, values follow row-major order.

face = 2 × (r // 16) + (c // 16) element_offset = 256 × face + 16 × (r % 16) + (c % 16) byte_offset = element_offset × bytes_per_element

For BF16, value (0,16) has element offset 256 and byte offset 512. A 32×32 FP32 tile uses the same face order and occupies 4,096 bytes. Tilization converts a row-major tensor into this storage order; untilization reverses the conversion.

Read the source: Official tile layout and address diagrams ↗

Destination registers (DST)

DST is the destination register storage inside a Tensix core. Matrix operations accumulate results there. The SFPU reads and writes these values for vector operations. Packers read the completed results and write them to L1.

The 32 KiB store holds 16 tiles of 16-bit values or 8 tiles of 32-bit values. Double buffering splits it into two sections: math works on one while pack drains the other. Synchronization transfers ownership between these phases.

Element widthOne double-buffered section (16 KiB)Full-sync section (32 KiB)
16 bits8 tiles of 32×32 values16 tiles of 32×32 values
32 bits4 tiles of 32×32 values8 tiles of 32×32 values

For example, a 2×3 tile output block needs six destination tiles. With 32-bit destinations and double buffering, the four-tile section is too small to hold the whole block at once. The compiler schedules smaller groups or uses additional storage. The IR & assembly chapter explains how the compiler schedules these groups.

Read the source: DST synchronization and configuration ↗ · DST physical storage ↗

02 / TT-Lang

Programming with TT-Lang

A one-tile addition example shows how host code launches cooperating device kernels.

In this chapter

Start with a program skeleton

We will add two 32×32 BF16 tiles. The host prepares three device tensors and calls one operation. That operation contains a reader, a compute kernel, and a writer.

Program skeleton · omitted bodies are expanded below
import ttl

# DEVICE DEFINITION — compiled by TT-Lang
@ttl.operation(grid=(1, 1))
def add_one_tile(a, b, out):
    # Declare three local queues: a_q, b_q, out_q.
    ...

    @ttl.datamovement()
    def reader():
        ...  # a, b → a_q, b_q

    @ttl.compute()
    def compute():
        ...  # a_q + b_q → out_q

    @ttl.datamovement()
    def writer():
        ...  # out_q → out

# HOST INVOCATION — device tensors supplied by the runner
add_one_tile(a_device, b_device, out_device)

The decorated definition is written in Python and processed on the host. TT-Lang compiles its kernel bodies into device programs. The call at the bottom launches the operation; the host calls add_one_tile once, and the device kernels cooperate through the queues.

Host programDevice program
Prepare inputs and device tensorsReader transfers inputs into local queues.
Invoke add_one_tile(a, b, out)Compute adds acquired input blocks.
Wait, read back, and check the resultWriter transfers the result to the output tensor.

Host code: prepare, invoke, and check

The host is the CPU process running the platform’s server-side runner. It initializes the accelerator, prepares the input values, allocates tiled device tensors, and uploads the inputs. It also allocates the output tensor before the operation is called.

Server-side host workflow · pseudocode
# Host workflow — pseudocode for course-runner services
initialize the assigned accelerator
prepare a_host and b_host: shape (32, 32), dtype BF16
allocate a_device, b_device, out_device: tiled device storage
upload a_host → a_device and b_host → b_device

# Actual TT-Lang invocation
add_one_tile(a_device, b_device, out_device)

wait for device completion
read out_device back into host row-major storage
compare with a_host + b_host using the required tolerance
release device resources

a_device, b_device, and out_device are handles to device tensors. Their shape, format, and placement describe the storage the operation will use. add_one_tile writes into out_device and returns None.

For this example, both inputs contain exactly 1,024 values, so no padding is needed. The host reference uses the same BF16-rounded inputs. The runner waits for completion before reading the result or stopping an execution timer.

Host invocation: compilation and specialization

The runner passes preallocated tensors to an operation. Shape, dtype, layout, and memory properties determine its specialization; tensor values are supplied at runtime. Calls with the same specialization can reuse the compiled program with new tensor values.

Block sizes, grid dimensions, and other scalar settings are compile-time values captured from an enclosing scope or factory function. Changing a block size therefore selects a new compiled program. The examples pass tensors as runtime arguments and capture scalar settings in the enclosing scope.

LevelExampleResponsibility
Host runnerAllocate tensors, invoke operation, check outputsDevice setup, transfers, validation, and timing boundaries.
Operation definitionDeclare DFBs and kernelsShared resources and execution structure.
Device kernel bodyLoop over tile coordinates, acquire blocks, copy or computeSupported DSL syntax lowered by the compiler.

The course runner handles host setup and invokes the operation. Importing a kernel file defines it; invocation triggers compilation and execution as needed.

Device code: the operation and its queues

@ttl.operation(grid=(1, 1)) selects one execution node. The outer function declares resources shared by the nested kernels. Each @ttl.datamovement() body describes transfer and synchronization work; the @ttl.compute() body describes arithmetic on blocks.

Device definition · shared buffers
@ttl.operation(grid=(1, 1))
def add_one_tile(a, b, out):
    a_q = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(a, shape=(1, 1), block_count=2)
    b_q = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(b, shape=(1, 1), block_count=2)
    out_q = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(out, shape=(1, 1), block_count=2)
    # The three kernel definitions below are nested here.

A dataflow buffer (DFB) is a local queue of blocks. Here shape=(1, 1) means one 32×32 tile per block, and block_count=2 gives the queue two slots. The corresponding tensor supplies the element format. Each BF16 slot holds 2,048 payload bytes.

a, b → reader → a_q, b_q → compute → out_q → writer → out

The reader produces blocks for compute. Compute produces blocks for the writer. The kernels can progress independently when their input blocks and output slots are available. Their definition order in the source establishes the program structure; queue dependencies determine when work can proceed.

Device reader: bring in the operands

Inside add_one_tile · reader kernel
@ttl.datamovement()
def reader():
    with a_q.reserve() as a_blk, b_q.reserve() as b_blk:
        a_request = ttl.copy(a[0, 0], a_blk)
        b_request = ttl.copy(b[0, 0], b_blk)
        a_request.wait()
        b_request.wait()

reserve() waits for a free queue slot and gives the reader a writable block. a[0, 0] selects the first tile of the device tensor. ttl.copy starts a transfer into the reserved block and returns a request; request.wait() waits for that transfer to finish.

Leaving each reserve scope publishes its completed block. Compute can then acquire it. Both requests are issued before either wait, allowing the two input transfers to overlap.

Device compute: add the blocks

Inside add_one_tile · compute kernel
@ttl.compute()
def compute():
    with a_q.wait() as a_blk, b_q.wait() as b_blk:
        with out_q.reserve() as out_blk:
            out_blk.store(a_blk + b_blk)

a_q.wait() and b_q.wait() acquire published input blocks. Reserving out_q obtains space for the result. The expression a_blk + b_blk describes elementwise addition of all 1,024 values, and store materializes the result in the output block.

Closing the output scope publishes the result. Closing the input scopes releases those slots so the reader can reuse them. TT-Lang lowers this body into the required unpack, math, and pack work on the Tensix core.

Device writer: store the result

Inside add_one_tile · writer kernel
@ttl.datamovement()
def writer():
    with out_q.wait() as out_blk:
        ttl.copy(out_blk, out[0, 0]).wait()

The writer acquires a completed block from out_q, copies it into the output device tensor, and waits for the copy to finish. Leaving the scope releases the queue slot. The result is now in out; the host runner handles completion and readback.

The two uses of wait refer to different events: out_q.wait() waits for a published block, while the request returned by ttl.copy waits for a transfer to complete.

Complete device operation

Putting the declarations and three kernel bodies together gives the operation below. The host invokes it with the three preallocated tensors from the skeleton.

Teaching adaptation · one-tile addition
import ttl

@ttl.operation(grid=(1, 1))
def add_one_tile(a, b, out):
    a_q = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(a, shape=(1, 1), block_count=2)
    b_q = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(b, shape=(1, 1), block_count=2)
    out_q = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(out, shape=(1, 1), block_count=2)

    @ttl.datamovement()
    def reader():
        with a_q.reserve() as a_blk, b_q.reserve() as b_blk:
            a_request = ttl.copy(a[0, 0], a_blk)
            b_request = ttl.copy(b[0, 0], b_blk)
            a_request.wait()
            b_request.wait()

    @ttl.compute()
    def compute():
        with a_q.wait() as a_blk, b_q.wait() as b_blk:
            with out_q.reserve() as out_blk:
                out_blk.store(a_blk + b_blk)

    @ttl.datamovement()
    def writer():
        with out_q.wait() as out_blk:
            ttl.copy(out_blk, out[0, 0]).wait()
  1. The reader reserves A and B storage, starts both copies, and waits for their bytes before scope exit publishes them.
  2. Compute acquires the input blocks and materializes their sum in the reserved output. Closing the scopes publishes output and releases inputs.
  3. The writer waits for output, completes its outbound copy, and then releases the slot.

The declared buffers occupy 3 × 2 × 2,048 = 12,288 payload bytes per node. This example needs only one slot per queue. We use two so the declarations can be reused when adding a loop and overlapping successive transfers.

Read the source: Official elementwise progression ↗ · Block and copy semantics ↗

Queue ownership: reserve, publish, acquire, release

make_dataflow_buffer_like(a,shape=(1,1),block_count=2) allocates scratch storage for two blocks on each participating node. The tensor supplies format information. Queue depth limits how far the producer can run ahead.

CallRoleMeaning
dfb.reserve()ProducerWait for capacity; acquire the next write block. Existing bytes are not guaranteed zero.
block.push()ProducerPublish a completed block.
dfb.wait()ConsumerWait for a published block; acquire the next read block.
block.pop()ConsumerRelease the block and return capacity.
Python · TT-Lang
with input_dfb.reserve() as tile:
    transfer = ttl.copy(a[0, 0], tile)
    transfer.wait()  # bytes have arrived
# reserve scope exit pushes the block

with input_dfb.wait() as tile:
    ...  # consume the block here
# wait scope exit pops the block

The wait completes the transfer, and leaving the reserve scope publishes the block. Both steps are needed before compute can consume the input. On an output queue, releasing a block before writeback completes would allow its storage to be overwritten too soon.

Tensor, tile, block, and grid shapes

ObjectExampleMeaning
Logical tensorA.shape=(64,128)64 scalar rows and 128 scalar columns.
Tile grid(2,4)Eight 32×32 tiles cover A.
DFB blockshape=(1,2)One acquired block covers 32×64 scalars.
Launch gridgrid=(2,2)Four execution nodes, each with local buffers.

In a data-movement kernel, a[m,k] indexes tiles. For example, a[0:2,1:3] selects a 2×2 tile block covering scalar rows 0–63 and columns 32–95. The a.shape property uses scalar dimensions. This difference matters when converting loop bounds into slice indices.

A 32×32 tile occupies 2,048 payload bytes in BF16 or 4,096 in FP32. Its four 16×16 faces are stored contiguously, as described in the architecture chapter. The host runtime performs tilization before the device kernel uses these tiles.

Shape and storage transformationsLoop tiling changes traversal. Tilization changes storage order. Padding changes physical extents. A kernel may require all three.

Padding requirements

For scalar extent D, tile padding gives Dp=32×ceil(D/32). Matmul padding along K must contribute zero to the dot product; output outside the logical result is cropped. Blocked kernels may require alignment to 32×BM,32×BN,32×BK, stricter than one tile.

Check A[65,97] × B[97,33]
Tile-only padding yields A[96,128], B[128,64], C[96,64], with six output tiles. For 2×2 output blocks and BK=2, pad M to 128 instead. Zero-fill the input extensions and crop C to[65,33].

Asynchrony and double buffering

ttl.copy returns a transfer request. Issuing the A and B requests before calling request.wait() allows their transfers to overlap, subject to the memory system and the chosen routes.

With two slots, the reader can fill block k+1 while compute consumes block k. With one slot, it must wait for compute to release that storage. Additional slots consume more L1 and help only while there is work available to overlap. All kernels on a core must agree on the stream order and block count.

Why does a queue not carry matrix coordinates?
The stream order encodes the coordinates. In the baseline, the reader produces (m,n,k) order and compute consumes it in the same order. Reordering one side alone pairs the wrong operands. A missing production or extra wait can hang.

L1 and DST requirements

For BF16 input blocks BM×BK and BK×BN, output BM×BN, and queue depth d, the three declared queues use:

L1 payload = 2,048 × d × (BM×BK + BK×BN + BM×BN) bytes

This estimate covers the three declared queue payloads. Alignment, compiler-created buffers, code, and runtime resources also use L1. Check the compiler’s allocation and budget diagnostics for the complete requirement.

DST has a smaller capacity than L1. Double-buffered 32-bit DST storage provides four 32×32 tiles per section. Full synchronization exposes eight tiles with less overlap. Consequently, a block that fits in L1 may still need DST subblocking.

Read the source: Compute configuration and DST ↗

Work assignment

ttl.node(dims=1) gives a flattened logical node index; ttl.grid_size(dims=1) gives the number of nodes. A simple assignment gives node p the block IDs p, p+P, p+2P, …. Every kernel on that node must use the same ownership rule and traversal order.

For Q=10 blocks and P=4 nodes, the assignments are [0,4,8], [1,5,9], [2,6], and [3,7]. This covers each block once, but workloads with unequal block costs can still be imbalanced. Logical coordinates are mapped by the runtime; do not use them as raw NoC coordinates.

For 2D grids, name the axes explicitly. The official matmul tutorial uses grid coordinates ordered as N then M. Swapping those meanings changes which output rectangle each node owns.

Read the source: Grid and node APIs ↗ · Full-grid matmul source ↗

Local queues and cross-node pipes

A DFB connects kernels on one node. A ttl.Pipe describes a connection between nodes, and ttl.PipeNet groups these connections into a communication pattern. A multicast receiver still needs to reserve space before the sender transfers a block.

Cross-node transfers add dependencies between the sender and receivers; each receiver publishes a block after its transfer completes.

Read the source: Pipe specification ↗ · 2D multicast example ↗

Matrix multiplication

Compare single-core, larger-block, and multicore matmul implementations.

In this chapter
1. Matmul animation2. Single core3. Larger blocks4. Multicore

1. Matmul animation

For A[64,128] and B[128,96], each output tile accumulates four products of 32×32 tiles; select an output and step through K.

Trace one output tile

64 × 128 @ 128 × 96

Select C, then advance through K. Highlighted A and B tiles feed the selected output.

2. Single core

The submission platform supplies tiled BF16 tensors A[M,K], B[K,N], and out[M,N], with dimensions divisible by 32. One core computes one output tile at a time: the reader supplies input tiles, compute accumulates across K, and the writer stores the result.

Single core · matmul.py
import ttl


@ttl.operation(grid=(1, 1))
def matmul(a, b, out):
    M, K, N = a.shape[0], a.shape[1], b.shape[1]
    assert M > 0 and K > 0 and N > 0
    assert K == b.shape[0]
    assert out.shape[0] == M and out.shape[1] == N
    assert M % 32 == 0 and K % 32 == 0 and N % 32 == 0
    Mt, Kt, Nt = M // 32, K // 32, N // 32

    a_dfb = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(a, shape=(1, 1), block_count=2)
    b_dfb = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(b, shape=(1, 1), block_count=2)
    out_dfb = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(out, shape=(1, 1), block_count=2)

    @ttl.datamovement()
    def reader():
        for m in range(Mt):
            for n in range(Nt):
                for k in range(Kt):
                    with a_dfb.reserve() as a_blk, b_dfb.reserve() as b_blk:
                        tx_a = ttl.copy(a[m, k], a_blk)
                        tx_b = ttl.copy(b[k, n], b_blk)
                        tx_a.wait()
                        tx_b.wait()

    @ttl.compute()
    def compute():
        for _ in range(Mt):
            for _ in range(Nt):
                with out_dfb.reserve() as out_blk:
                    acc = ttl.block.fill(0, shape=out_blk.shape)
                    for _ in range(Kt):
                        with a_dfb.wait() as a_blk, b_dfb.wait() as b_blk:
                            acc += a_blk @ b_blk
                    out_blk.store(acc)

    @ttl.datamovement()
    def writer():
        for m in range(Mt):
            for n in range(Nt):
                with out_dfb.wait() as out_blk:
                    ttl.copy(out_blk, out[m, n]).wait()

3. Larger blocks

Keep one core and set BM=BN=BK=2, so each block spans 64×64 values. The loop structure stays the same; larger slices reuse inputs across four output tiles. Use dimensions divisible by 64.

Larger blocks on one core · matmul_larger.py
import ttl

BM, BN, BK = 2, 2, 2


@ttl.operation(grid=(1, 1))
def matmul_larger(a, b, out):
    M, K, N = a.shape[0], a.shape[1], b.shape[1]
    assert M > 0 and K > 0 and N > 0
    assert K == b.shape[0]
    assert out.shape[0] == M and out.shape[1] == N
    assert M % (32 * BM) == 0 and K % (32 * BK) == 0
    assert N % (32 * BN) == 0
    Mt, Kt, Nt = M // (32 * BM), K // (32 * BK), N // (32 * BN)

    a_dfb = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(a, shape=(BM, BK), block_count=2)
    b_dfb = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(b, shape=(BK, BN), block_count=2)
    out_dfb = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(out, shape=(BM, BN), block_count=2)

    @ttl.datamovement()
    def reader():
        for m in range(Mt):
            for n in range(Nt):
                for k in range(Kt):
                    with a_dfb.reserve() as a_blk, b_dfb.reserve() as b_blk:
                        tx_a = ttl.copy(a[m*BM:(m+1)*BM, k*BK:(k+1)*BK], a_blk)
                        tx_b = ttl.copy(b[k*BK:(k+1)*BK, n*BN:(n+1)*BN], b_blk)
                        tx_a.wait()
                        tx_b.wait()

    @ttl.compute()
    def compute():
        for _ in range(Mt):
            for _ in range(Nt):
                with out_dfb.reserve() as out_blk:
                    acc = ttl.block.fill(0, shape=out_blk.shape)
                    for _ in range(Kt):
                        with a_dfb.wait() as a_blk, b_dfb.wait() as b_blk:
                            acc += a_blk @ b_blk
                    out_blk.store(acc)

    @ttl.datamovement()
    def writer():
        for m in range(Mt):
            for n in range(Nt):
                with out_dfb.wait() as out_blk:
                    ttl.copy(out_blk, out[m*BM:(m+1)*BM, n*BN:(n+1)*BN]).wait()

4. Multicore

Keep the same block sizes and use grid="matmul-full". Divide the output blocks among cores; each core runs its own reader, compute, and writer over the same assigned blocks. The q < mb * nb guard skips unused assignments.

Larger blocks across cores · matmul_blocked.py
import ttl

BM, BN, BK = 2, 2, 2


@ttl.operation(grid="full")
def matmul_blocked(a, b, out):
    M, K, N = a.shape[0], a.shape[1], b.shape[1]
    assert M > 0 and K > 0 and N > 0
    assert K == b.shape[0]
    assert out.shape[0] == M and out.shape[1] == N
    assert M % (32 * BM) == 0 and N % (32 * BN) == 0
    assert K % (32 * BK) == 0
    mb, nb, kb = M // (32 * BM), N // (32 * BN), K // (32 * BK)
    cores = ttl.grid_size(dims=1)
    per_core = (mb * nb + cores - 1) // cores
    a_dfb = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(a, shape=(BM, BK), block_count=2)
    b_dfb = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(b, shape=(BK, BN), block_count=2)
    out_dfb = ttl.make_dataflow_buffer_like(out, shape=(BM, BN), block_count=2)

    @ttl.datamovement()
    def reader():
        node = ttl.node(dims=1)
        for local in range(per_core):
            q = node * per_core + local
            if q < mb * nb:
                m, n = q // nb, q % nb
                for k in range(kb):
                    with a_dfb.reserve() as aa, b_dfb.reserve() as bb:
                        ta = ttl.copy(a[m*BM:(m+1)*BM, k*BK:(k+1)*BK], aa)
                        tb = ttl.copy(b[k*BK:(k+1)*BK, n*BN:(n+1)*BN], bb)
                        ta.wait()
                        tb.wait()

    @ttl.compute()
    def compute():
        node = ttl.node(dims=1)
        for local in range(per_core):
            q = node * per_core + local
            if q < mb * nb:
                with out_dfb.reserve() as cc:
                    acc = ttl.block.fill(0, shape=cc.shape)
                    for _ in range(kb):
                        with a_dfb.wait() as aa, b_dfb.wait() as bb:
                            acc += aa @ bb
                    cc.store(acc)

    @ttl.datamovement()
    def writer():
        node = ttl.node(dims=1)
        for local in range(per_core):
            q = node * per_core + local
            if q < mb * nb:
                m, n = q // nb, q % nb
                with out_dfb.wait() as cc:
                    ttl.copy(cc, out[m*BM:(m+1)*BM, n*BN:(n+1)*BN]).wait()

04 / IR & assembly

Compiler stages and inspection tools

Use the compiler tools to follow a kernel from TT-Lang source to device code.

In this chapter
Compilation stagesExample IR and C++Inspection toolsExample commands

Compilation stages

TT-Lang Python→TTL IR→TTKernel IR→EmitC IR→Kernel C++→Device ELF
StagePurpose
Frontend → TTL IRSpecialize the Python operation and represent its computation, data movement, and control flow in MLIR.
TTL IR → TTKernel IRLower block operations and dataflow into operations for device kernel APIs.
TTKernel IR → EmitC IR → C++Express the lowered program as C++ calls and generate device-kernel source.
C++ → device ELFCompile and link the generated kernels with the Tenstorrent device toolchain. The resulting ELF files contain executable code for the assigned device processors.

IR dumps, generated C++, and disassembly show different points along this path. Disassembly is obtained by decoding a device ELF.

Read the source: TT-Lang compiler pipeline ↗ · Device compilation ↗

Example IR and C++

A single-tile matmul multiplies two 32×32 BF16 tiles. This shortened TTL excerpt comes from an upstream lowering test; buffer declarations and the surrounding function are omitted.

TTL IR · excerpt from a compiler test
%mm = ttl.matmul %a, %b
    : tensor<1x1x!ttcore.tile<32x32, bf16>>,
      tensor<1x1x!ttcore.tile<32x32, bf16>>
   -> tensor<1x1x!ttcore.tile<32x32, bf16>>
ttl.store %mm, %reserve
    : tensor<1x1x!ttcore.tile<32x32, bf16>>,
      tensor<1x1x!ttcore.tile<32x32, bf16>>

%a and %b are input values; %mm is the result. The outer 1x1 counts tiles, and 32x32 gives the elements in each tile. ttl.store writes the result into the reserved output block.

Kernel C++ · illustrative adaptation
// Illustrative C++ excerpt; buffer IDs have descriptive names.
// Hardware initialization and queue operations are omitted.
tile_regs_acquire();
matmul_block_init(cb_a, cb_b, 0, 1, 1, 1);
matmul_block(cb_a, cb_b, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1);
tile_regs_commit();
tile_regs_wait();
pack_tile(0, cb_out, 0);
tile_regs_release();

The lowered code makes register ownership, matrix-engine work, and output packing explicit. The final three arguments of matmul_block are the output columns, output rows, and inner dimension in tiles; all are one here. pack_tile writes the result from destination registers to the output circular buffer. This excerpt illustrates the API calls; it has not been captured from a compilation of the tutorial kernel.

Read the source: One-tile lowering test ↗ · Matmul API ↗

Inspection tools

Compiler options in Python

TT-Lang provides compiler options that you can set in Python scripts. List the available options with:

Python · list compiler options
from ttl.compiler_options import CompilerOptions

print(CompilerOptions.usage())

Pass a string of options to @ttl.operation:

Python · operation configuration; kernel body omitted
import ttl

@ttl.operation(grid=(1, 1), options="--no-ttl-maximize-dst")
def matmul(a, b, out):
    # Reader, compute, and writer definitions go here.
    ...

You can also supply options= when calling an existing operation:

Python · options for one invocation
# a_device, b_device, and out_device are prepared device tensors.
matmul(
    a_device, b_device, out_device,
    options="--no-ttl-maximize-dst --no-ttl-combine-pack-tiles",
)

The call-time string replaces the decorator’s option string for that invocation. Environment and command-line settings can override these values.

Common compiler options

OptionDefaultEffect
--ttl-maximize-dstEnabledGroup tile work to use destination registers efficiently. Use --no-ttl-maximize-dst to compare per-tile synchronization.
--ttl-fpu-binary-opsEnabledAllow eligible add, subtract, and multiply operations to use the matrix engine. --no-ttl-fpu-binary-ops selects the vector engine.
--ttl-combine-pack-tilesEnabledCombine consecutive output-packing operations. Use --no-ttl-combine-pack-tiles to disable this transformation.
--ttl-subblock-syncDisabledSynchronize individual subblocks within a larger block.
--ttl-accumulation-strategy autoautoChoose accumulation storage automatically; dst and l1-pack select destination registers and L1-backed accumulation, respectively.

The Python compiler also reads these environment variables:

Environment variablePurpose
TTLANG_INITIAL_MLIR=initial.mlirWrite MLIR before the compiler pipeline to this file.
TTLANG_FINAL_MLIR=final.mlirWrite MLIR after the compiler pipeline to this file.
TTLANG_VERBOSE_PASSES=1Print IR after each compiler pass.
TTLANG_DEBUG_LOCATIONS=1Include source locations in printed MLIR.

Read the source: Python option parser ↗ · Compiler options ↗

ttlang-opt

The standalone MLIR optimizer reads an MLIR file and runs passes. It accepts standard MLIR driver options, including the two IR-printing flags below.

OptionPurpose
--helpList the options and passes available in this installation.
-p 'ttl-to-ttkernel-pipeline'Run the registered TT-Lang lowering pipeline.
--mlir-print-ir-before-allPrint IR before each pass.
--mlir-print-ir-after-allPrint IR after each pass.
-o lowered.mlirWrite the resulting IR to a file.

Read the source: ttlang-opt reference ↗ · MLIR IR printing ↗

ttlang-translate

Translate prepared kernel IR into C++ source.

OptionPurpose

Example commands

The following examples illustrate the tool interfaces. Input files and tool paths stand for artifacts and tools from the same compiler installation.

Compiler tools
# Print the IR after each pass in a registered pipeline.
ttlang-opt input.mlir -p 'ttl-to-ttkernel-pipeline' \
  --mlir-print-ir-after-all -o lowered.mlir 2> passes.log

# Translate IR prepared for C++ emission.
ttlang-translate --ttkernel-to-cpp emitc.mlir -o kernel.cpp
Binary tools
# Inspect one processor binary with its matching toolchain.
/path/to/sfpi/compiler/bin/riscv-tt-elf-readelf -h -S -s kernel.elf
/path/to/sfpi/compiler/bin/riscv-tt-elf-objdump -d kernel.elf > kernel.disasm

Use filenames and processor labels to keep related artifacts together. A reader, writer, and compute program can produce separate binaries.

06 / Practice 2

Ragged sum

Sum the valid prefix of each row.

In this chapter
Problem definitionExamplesPyTorch baselineTest shapes

Problem definition

TensorData typeShape
xtorch.float32[R, L]
lengthstorch.int64[R]

R ≥ 1 and L ≥ 1. Row r contains lengths[r] valid values, with 0 ≤ lengths[r] ≤ L. Only x[r, :lengths[r]] contributes to the result. Entries beyond that prefix may be nonzero. All inputs are on the same device.

All values in x are finite. Return a torch.float32 tensor of shape [R], where out[r] = sum(x[r, :lengths[r]]). An empty row returns zero.

Row lengthOutput
0The valid interval [0, 0) is empty; return 0.
1Return x[r, 0].
LSum all L values. The unused tail [L, L) is empty.

Examples

Example 1
# Input
x = [
    [1, 2, 9],
    [4, -1, 8],
    [7, 8, 9]
]
lengths = [2, 1, 0]

# Output
out = [3, 4, 0]
Example 2
# Input
x = [
    [0.5, -0.5, 2, -1],
    [-2, -3, 9, 9]
]
lengths = [4, 2]

# Output
out = [1, -5]

Only the prefix specified by each row length contributes; a row of length zero returns zero.

PyTorch baseline

Python · PyTorch
import torch

def ragged_sum_reference(x: torch.Tensor, lengths: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    # x: float32 [R, L]; lengths: int64 [R]; result: float32 [R]
    columns = torch.arange(x.shape[1], device=x.device)
    valid = columns[None, :] < lengths[:, None]
    values = x.masked_fill(~valid, 0.0)
    return values.sum(dim=1)

Inputs, accumulation, and output use FP32.

07 / Practice 3

Ragged softmax

Apply softmax to the valid prefix of each row.

In this chapter
Problem definitionExamplesPyTorch baselineTest shapes

Problem definition

TensorData typeShape
xtorch.float32[R, L]
lengthstorch.int64[R]

R ≥ 1 and L ≥ 1. Row r contains lengths[r] valid values, with 0 ≤ lengths[r] ≤ L. Only x[r, :lengths[r]] contributes to the result. Entries beyond that prefix may be nonzero. All inputs are on the same device.

All values in x are finite and lie in [-80, 80]. Return a torch.float32 tensor of shape [R, L]. For each nonempty row, out[r, :lengths[r]] = softmax(x[r, :lengths[r]]). All remaining entries, including every entry of an empty row, must be zero.

Row lengthOutput
0The valid interval [0, 0) is empty; return an all-zero row of length L.
1Return 1 at index zero and 0 in the remaining entries.
LApply softmax to all L values. The tail [L, L) has no entries to fill.

Intervals are half-open: [a, b) includes a and excludes b. An interval with equal endpoints contains no elements. The output still has shape [R, L].

Examples

Example 1
# Input
x = [
    [2, 2, 80],
    [-3, 9, 9],
    [7, 8, 9]
]
lengths = [2, 1, 0]

# Output
out = [
    [0.5, 0.5, 0],
    [1, 0, 0],
    [0, 0, 0]
]
Example 2
# Input
x = [
    [0, 1, 80]
]
lengths = [2]

# Output
out = [
    [0.26894143, 0.7310586, 0]
]

Entries outside the valid prefix are zero. The second output shows FP32 probabilities rounded to eight decimal places.

PyTorch baseline

Python · PyTorch
import torch

def ragged_softmax_reference(x: torch.Tensor, lengths: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    # x: float32 [R, L]; lengths: int64 [R]; result: float32 [R, L]
    columns = torch.arange(x.shape[1], device=x.device)
    valid = columns[None, :] < lengths[:, None]
    logits = x.masked_fill(~valid, -torch.inf)
    # Give empty rows finite logits before softmax; zero them below.
    logits = torch.where(lengths[:, None] > 0, logits, 0.0)
    result = torch.softmax(logits, dim=1).masked_fill(~valid, 0.0)
    return result

Inputs, softmax computation, and output use FP32.

1. Time reporting — 20 points

  • Use figures or tables to report execution times for all 10 cases of each exercise. Label the exercise, case, implementation, time unit, and submission ID.
  • Compare your initial correct implementation with your final implementation. Report speedup as initial time / final time, using the same timing scope. Label missing or failed results.
  • Use the measurements returned by the submission platform and state what its reported time includes.

2. Implementation sketch — 20 points

  • For each exercise, give concise pseudocode or a diagram of your final implementation.
  • Describe work assignment, data movement, and computation. Explain how the implementation handles irregular sizes, empty rows, and singleton rows where applicable.

3. Optimization and profiling metric analysis — 20 points

  • For each exercise, explain at least one change from the initial implementation, the cost it targets, and its effect on execution time across cases.
  • Analyze the profiling metrics returned by the platform. Give each metric’s name, unit, scope, and before/after values, and explain how it supports or challenges your hypothesis.
  • Discuss a regression or a case with little improvement. If a relevant metric is unavailable, identify it and explain what it would help determine; separate measured results from hypotheses.

4. IR analysis — 40 points

Answer all eight questions. Each is worth 5 points out of 100. Use the named functions and CHECK expectations in the supplied compiler tests; cite file names and line numbers. These questions can be answered from the linked sources and compiler tests without running a kernel.

MLIR files for the questions

Q1. Host and device compilation paths — 5 points

Provide a table of the compilation and execution stages, in sequence, from a TT-Lang Python operation call to execution on the accelerator. Use four columns: stage, execution hardware (CPU or accelerator), input, and output.

Q2. Tensor types and dimensions — 5 points

In matmul_to_compute.mlir, inspect matmul_2x4_4x3. Write the full types, tile dimensions, and number of tiles of the two input tensors and the result.

Q3. Iteration space and indexing maps — 5 points

For matmul_2x4_4x3 in matmul_to_compute.mlir, explain the three affine indexing maps for A, B, and the output.

Q4. Circular-buffer capacities — 5 points

In matmul_2x4_4x3 in matmul_block_lowering.mlir, identify the three ttl.bind_cb declarations and their block_count values. Calculate each buffer’s capacity in tiles and BF16 payload bytes. Match the tile capacities to the !ttkernel.cb types in the CHECK expectations; count payload only.

Q5. Register and packing sequence — 5 points

In the CHECK expectations for matmul_1x1_bf16 in matmul_block_lowering.mlir, list the operations from tile_regs_acquire through tile_regs_release in order. Identify the matrix operation and the operation that writes the result to the output buffer. Explain the roles of commit and wait in this sequence.

Q6. Reduction loop after lowering — 5 points

In the CHECK expectations for matmul_2x4_4x3 in matmul_block_lowering.mlir, give the scf.for lower and upper bounds. Using the input-index expressions stated in the fixture, list the tile-index pairs passed to matmul_block over the K iterations. Give the ct, rt, and kt arguments, and identify which register-ownership operations remain outside the loop.

Q7. Pack-combining transformation — 5 points

Compare CHECK and COMBINED for matmul_2x4_4x3 in matmul_block_lowering.mlir. Name the extra pass in the second RUN line. Count the packing operations before and after it, name their operation types, and state the destination-register and output-buffer tile ranges they cover. Explain why the 1x1 case keeps its existing packing operation.

Q8. Commands for inspecting IR — 5 points

Using the IR & assembly chapter, answer the following questions (1 point each). Give the option or command and briefly explain its output. You do not need to run the commands.

  1. Which environment variable saves the initial MLIR from a TT-Lang Python invocation?
  2. Which environment variable saves the final MLIR from that invocation?
  3. Which environment variable prints IR after each pass in the Python compiler pipeline?
  4. Which environment variable includes source locations in printed MLIR?

Instructor setup

  1. Pin the TT-Lang compiler, device runtime, SFPI, driver, firmware, and runner image for the course target.
  2. Provide a host runner that allocates tiled tensors, creates exact masks, invokes the submitted operation, synchronizes, crops/unpacks results, and checks outputs. Kernels import ttl; host allocation belongs to the runner.
  3. Enable TT-Lang submission contracts on the OJ. Existing problem interfaces may need changes to accept these kernels.
  4. Compile and validate each baseline on small shapes. Calibrate per-operation tolerances and confirm allocation budgets before releasing the large cases.
  5. For long ragged cases, validate an instructor streaming implementation; the provided full-row baseline intentionally stops at width 256.
  6. Capture a matched matmul source/IR/C++/ELF/disassembly bundle. Record actual artifact paths and tool versions.
  7. Publish timing boundaries, warmup/sample counts, problem IDs, report-upload route, and final grading weights.
